NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding

Nilesh Prasad Pandey Note: Both authors contributed equally to this research. email: nppandey@ucsd.edu Affiliation: University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA , Jangseon Park email: jap036@ucsd.edu Affiliation: University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA , Jason Kong email: jckong@ucsd.edu Affiliation: University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA , Onat Gungor email: onat.gungor@mail.wvu.edu Affiliation: West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA and Tajana Rosing email: tajana@ucsd.edu Affiliation: University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA
© none
Abstract.

Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt nn-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j,b)(j,b), consisting of the accepted draft length jj and target-emitted continuation token bb. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99×1.99\times more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0×7.0\times more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38×1.38\times over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40×1.40\times overlap ceiling.

Keywords: 
reinforcement learning, large language models, speculative decoding, n-gram caching, CPU–GPU co-design

1. Introduction

Reinforcement learning post-training (Ouyang et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2017), and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in particular (Shao et al., 2024), has become central to improving LLM reasoning (Guo et al., 2025). But it is expensive, and the cost is dominated by the rollout generation. Each GRPO step autoregressively samples many completions per prompt before any gradient is computed, and this phase alone can exceed 70% of step time (Ji et al., 2025). Accelerating rollout is therefore the most direct route to reducing the RL post-training cost. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) offers a natural solution for improving the efficiency of RL using a small drafter that proposes tokens which the target model verifies in parallel, preserving the target’s exact output distribution. However, this mechanism does not transfer cleanly to the RL rollout setting, for two reasons. First, a separate draft model or a set of trained draft heads (Li et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024) consumes GPU memory alongside the policy, optimizer states, and KV cache, and must itself be trained and maintained, an added cost precisely where memory and compute are already scarce. Second, such drafters degrade over training. As the policy drifts, a fixed drafter’s proposals are increasingly rejected (Liu et al., 2023), so acceptance falls over exactly the long horizons on which RL runs. To overcome these issues, model-free drafters (Saxena, 2023; He et al., 2024) remove the additional memory cost by reusing tokens from the prompt or a datastore rather than predicting them, but their draft candidates are confined to a single generation, due to which acceptance stays low on the adapting traces that RL post-training produces.

Our key insight is that during RL training, the rollout already contains its own drafter, for free. Because GRPO revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between steps, a prompt’s completions are highly repetitive with those generated for it earlier in training. Prior rollouts are thus a self-updating source of draft tokens requiring no extra parameters, no training, and automatically tracking the policy since they are produced by it. This repetition is especially strong for structured tasks, whose outputs are regular by construction, and it arises across rollouts of the same prompt over training, a signal that previous model-free drafters, which draw only on a single generation, cannot exploit (Saxena, 2023; He et al., 2024).

Exploiting this signal, however, raises a systems problem. A model-free cache carries no GPU memory cost precisely because it lives on the CPU, but a naive integration then serializes the CPU lookup with the GPU forward: the GPU stalls on the host every decode step while the next draft is looked up and the step is scheduled. In our measurements this host round trip idles the GPU for nearly a third of each iteration, and the cache lookup is a negligible part of it; the synchronization and scheduling dominate. Realizing the cache’s benefit therefore requires co-designing the drafter with the rollout engine so that the host work is hidden behind the GPU, not merely making the lookup fast.

To this end, we propose NgramRL, a rollout-aware per-prompt n-gram cache that acts as a model-free drafter for speculative decoding during RL post-training. For each prompt, NgramRL maintains an n-gram table built from that prompt’s prior rollouts and proposes continuations by lookup, which the policy verifies. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, overlapping GPU computation so that drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and negligible GPU time, and because it is populated by the policy’s own outputs it stays aligned with the policy rather than going stale like a fixed drafter. To keep this CPU work off the critical path, NgramRL pairs the cache with an asynchronous multipath prefetch runtime that prefetches the next step’s drafts during verification, so the decode iteration collapses to GPU busy time.

We make the following contributions:

  • •

    We identify and characterize prompt-conditioned temporal locality in RL rollouts. GRPO repeatedly samples the same prompts while updating the policy incrementally, previous rollouts provide high-quality drafts for future epochs. Across consecutive epochs, a prior rollout covers 48-96% of a later rollout, with recurring spans of 7-23 tokens.

  • •

    We propose NgramRL, a self-updating, per-prompt nn-gram drafter constructed entirely from recent policy rollouts. Its bounded-history design limits host-memory growth and reduces mismatch with the evolving policy, while requiring no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state.

  • •

    We design an adaptive fan-out prefetcher, guided by a causal budget allocator, that speculatively prepares next-step drafts for likely verification outcomes (j,b)(j,b) during the forward. Covered outcomes bypass the verification-dependent host round trip; uncovered requests fall back to sequential lookup without altering the target-emitted token or rollout distribution.

  • •

    Across two model families and three workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99×1.99\times more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0×7.0\times more than prompt-lookup decoding. At N=16N=16, the prefetcher covers up to 99.5% of Spider outcomes and delivers up to 1.38×1.38\times measured rollout speedup over synchronous NgramRL.

2. Background and Related Work

2.1. Background: The Rollout Bottleneck

A GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) training step consists of three stages. The policy samples a group of completions (rollouts) for each prompt, a reward model scores them, and the policy is updated from the group-relative advantages. The first stage, rollout, dominates the wall-clock cost. Completions are produced autoregressively, one token at a time, and this stage alone can exceed 70% of step time (Ji et al., 2025). Production frameworks such as verl (Sheng et al., 2025) therefore delegate rollout to a dedicated inference engine (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024). Speculative decoding is the natural way to accelerate it, but three properties of the RL setting make existing variants not well-suited for this problem.

(C1) First, GPU memory is already saturated. The policy, optimizer states, gradients, and KV cache contend for device memory during training. A speculative scheme that introduces a draft model or trained draft heads adds a persistent claim on the limited GPU resource, and can incur additional GPU-side speculation cost (Chen et al., 2024). (C2) Second, the target is non-stationary. Existing speculative decoding assumes a fixed target, whereas RL updates the policy at every step. A drafter trained against one snapshot is therefore stale at the next, and its acceptance declines as the policy drifts (Liu et al., 2023). (C3) Third, rollouts are free-form yet repetitive across steps. Reasoning traces rarely have much overlap with the prompt, so drafters that copy from the current context find few matches. The repetition instead lies across training steps, where the same prompts recur, and hence single-generation drafters fail to use this characteristic. NgramRL is designed to satisfy C1–C3 at once.

2.2. Related Work

Model-based speculative decoding. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) pairs a fast drafter with the target, which verifies drafted tokens in parallel while preserving the target’s output distribution. Strong methods train the drafter as a separate draft model, additional decoding heads such as Medusa (Cai et al., 2024), or feature-level draft models such as EAGLE (Li et al., 2024). The crucial difference between this literature and our work is that these drafters add trainable parameters and assume a fixed target. In RL post-training both assumptions fail, since the parameters consume scarce GPU memory and a fixed drafter cannot track a policy that changes every step.

Model-free drafters. A separate line copies previously seen tokens rather than predicting them. Prompt-lookup decoding (Saxena, 2023) matches nn-grams against the current prompt, REST (He et al., 2024) retrieves continuations from a fixed datastore, and Token Recycling (Luo et al., 2025) reuses candidates discarded during a single decode. These add no parameters, but their evidence is limited to a single generation or a static corpus, so acceptance is low on the free-form traces that RL produces. The closest work is SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2026), which caches token sequences from prior outputs in CPU-side suffix trees and performs best on structured tasks such as text-to-SQL. The crucial difference is the setting. SuffixDecoding serves a fixed model, and its repetition arises from agentic inference pipelines. We operate inside RL training, where the policy is non-stationary and the repetition arises from GRPO revisiting the same prompts. Our per-prompt cache consequently co-evolves with the policy, and acceptance strengthens as training proceeds, a behavior the fixed-target setting does not exhibit.

Structured generation. The highest-value targets for RL post-training, including text-to-SQL, code generation, and tool and API calls, produce outputs with strong syntactic regularity. Completions of the same prompt share schema tokens, keywords, and boilerplate, so identical tokens recur, and copy-based drafting is known to favor such low-entropy outputs (Oliaro et al., 2026). We show that this regularity is amplified in RL training, where the same prompts are sampled repeatedly, so structured tasks benefit most from rollout-derived nn-gram caching.

3. NgramRL: Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding

3.1. Overview

As shown in Figure 1, NgramRL is a co-design of a model-free drafter with the RL rollout engine. It accelerates rollout without adding parameters, training a draft model, or claiming persistent GPU memory.

The design rests on one property of RL post-training. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between them, so a prompt’s completions repeat those it produced earlier in training. Figure 2 illustrates this phenomenon: rollouts of the same Spider (Yu et al., 2018) (text-to-SQL) prompt one epoch apart share only the query skeleton early on and become verbatim identical by late training. NgramRL turns this redundancy into accepted drafts, a signal a single-generation drafter cannot utilize.

Each prompt owns an nn-gram cache built from its prior rollouts. During rollout the cache proposes continuations by lookup and the policy verifies them exactly, preserving the output distribution. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, so drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and overlaps GPU compute. The remaining subsections detail the cache, the draft-and-verify procedure, and the CPU-GPU co-design.

3.2. Per-Prompt N-gram Cache

Based on this insight, we design our proposed drafter as a set of per-prompt nn-gram look-up tables (LUTs), denoted 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p}. We keep one table per prompt rather than a single shared table, because rollouts of the same prompt are more repetitive with each other than rollouts of different prompts. The cache is built and maintained in two steps as summarized in Algorithm 1:

Cache Construction: For a prompt pp, let Rp(t)R_{p}^{(t)} be the rollouts sampled for pp at training step tt. After each step, we extract nn-grams of order nminn_{\min} to nmaxn_{\max} from these rollouts and insert them into the table 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p}, which maps each context of n−1n{-}1 tokens to its observed continuation and frequency. The orders nminn_{\min} and nmaxn_{\max} are a design choice, trading memory vs drafting quality.

Self-Updating Behavior: 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p} is rebuilt continually from the policy’s own recent rollouts, so as the policy updates its continuations converge toward the policy’s current preferences. The drafter thus tracks the policy without retraining. To bound table size and stay aligned with the latest policy, we retain rollouts from a recent window of WW steps and evict older entries.

3.3. Draft-and-Verify

Once the table is constructed, at every training step tt during the rollout of prompt pp, NgramRL proposes draft tokens from 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p} and the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} verifies them in one forward pass.

Draft Proposal: We query 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p} for the longest matching n-gram of the current context and propose its saved continuation as the draft token. If no match exists, the position falls back to standard decoding.

Verification Preserves the Policy: Let xx be the drafted token at a position with context cc. NgramRL accepts xx with probability

(1) pacc​(x)=min⁡(1,πθ​(x∣c)q⁡(x∣c)),p_{\text{acc}}(x)=\min\!\left(1,\ \frac{\pi_{\theta}(x\mid c)}{q(x\mid c)}\right),

where qq is the cache’s proposal distribution; on rejection, it resamples from the normalized positive residual (πθ(⋅∣c)−q(⋅∣c))+(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c)-q(\cdot\mid c))_{+}. This is the standard speculative-sampling correction (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), and it guarantees that the accepted token is distributed exactly as x∼πθ(⋅∣c)x\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c), independent of the drafter qq. Consequently the rollouts, rewards, advantages, and gradients are identical in distribution to non-speculative training, so NgramRL leaves accuracy and convergence unchanged.

3.4. N-Gram Prefetcher

Placing the cache on the CPU keeps it out of GPU memory but serializes the two processors. As Figure 3(a) shows, each decode iteration is a host–device round trip: the GPU verifies the draft, and only once the result is synchronized to the host can the CPU look up the next draft, schedule the step, and launch its kernels, leaving the GPU idle for ∼29%{\sim}29\% of every iteration. The lookup is a negligible part of this gap; the synchronization and scheduling dominate, so hiding the lookup alone is not enough. NgramRL therefore removes the whole round trip with a fan-out prefetcher that prepares the next step’s drafts during the current forward.

3.4.1. Adaptive Bonus-Token Fan-out Prefetcher

Overlapping the lookup with the forward is hard because the lookup context for step t+1t{+}1 is fixed only by the verification outcome of step tt, a pair (j,b)(j,b): the accept length j∈{0,…,k}j\in\{0,\dots,k\} and the bonus token bb the target emits at position j+1j{+}1 (resampled on a rejection, or the free token after a full accept). The accept length takes k+1k{+}1 values and is known to the CPU, but bb is sampled on the GPU from the full vocabulary and ends the next context, so it is unknown until verification finishes. Rather than discard bb, NgramRL predicts it, which keeps every committed token target-distributed and preserves the lossless guarantee of Section 3.3.

During step tt’s forward, the prefetcher builds a draft table for step t+1t{+}1 keyed by the outcome (j,b)(j,b). For each funded accept-length branch jj, it draws the top-fjf_{j} bonus candidates from 𝒞p\mathcal{C}_{p}, the frequency-ranked successors of the context extended by the jj accepted tokens, and issues one lookup per candidate to build the corresponding kk-token draft; the finished table is transferred to the GPU before the forward returns. Verification then yields the realized pair (j∗,b∗)(j^{*},b^{*}), which the GPU resolves by an O⁡(1)O(1) key probe with no content search. On a hit, with probability cc (the coverage), the selected draft is identical to the one the sequential design would have built, and decoding proceeds with no exposed host time; on a miss, the entry is discarded and only that request issues the ordinary sequential lookup, so misses never stall the batch. In either case the accepted prefix and the bonus token are committed unchanged, so NgramRL stays lossless (Eq. (1) holds) and degrades at worst to the synchronous baseline.

Adaptive budget allocation. The candidate budget N=∑jfjN{=}\sum_{j}f_{j} is split across branches from trailing statistics over a causal window of WW steps: the accept-length histogram P^​(j)\hat{P}(j) and each branch’s coverage profile c^j​(f)\hat{c}_{j}(f), the probability that the true bonus ranks within the top ff candidates. We maximize expected coverage,

(2) max⁡∑j{fj}⁡P^​(j)​c^j​(fj)s.t.∑jfj=N,\max_{\{f_{j}\}}\sum_{j}\hat{P}(j)\,\hat{c}_{j}(f_{j})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{j}f_{j}=N,

solved greedily by marginal gain. In effect the fan-out concentrates around the recent mode of the accept-length distribution, and full-accept branches, whose bonus is the next token of an already-cached trajectory and is the top candidate ∼90%{\sim}90\% of the time, need only one candidate (fj=1f_{j}{=}1), so a small budget covers high-acceptance tasks.

Cost. Let TgpuT_{\text{gpu}} be the device-busy time per iteration and TcpuT_{\text{cpu}} the serial host time it must hide. A covered iteration hides the host chain and a missed one pays it, giving

(3) speedup​(c)=Tgpu+TcpuTgpu+(1−c)​Tcpu→c→1 1+TcpuTgpu.\text{speedup}(c)=\frac{T_{\text{gpu}}+T_{\text{cpu}}}{T_{\text{gpu}}+(1-c)\,T_{\text{cpu}}}\;\xrightarrow{\,c\to 1\,}\;1+\frac{T_{\text{cpu}}}{T_{\text{gpu}}}.

The prefetch chain itself costs ≈N{\approx}N lookups per drafted request and must fit under TgpuT_{\text{gpu}}; beyond N≈64N{\approx}64 it approaches the host time TcpuT_{\text{cpu}} it hides, so the budget sweet spot is small (Section 4.1.5). Both the attainable speedup and the sweet spot are governed by the ratio Tcpu/TgpuT_{\text{cpu}}/T_{\text{gpu}}: larger models or larger batches raise TgpuT_{\text{gpu}} relative to the host chain, so the hidden overlap is a smaller fraction of each iteration, whereas CPU-heavier regimes benefit more.

3.5. Integration and Generality

We integrate NgramRL into verl’s (Sheng et al., 2025) vLLM rollout worker. The cache attaches to the rollout engine and needs no change to the reward model, optimizer, or policy architecture, so it is a drop-in optimization. Adding no parameters and no training, it composes with existing rollout-efficiency methods and applies to any RL-style setup where prompts recur.

4. Results

4.1. Experimental Setup

4.1.1. RL Training Setup

For all our experiments, we use verl (Sheng et al., 2025) for GRPO training (Shao et al., 2024), running on 2×2{\times} NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. The rollouts are served by the vLLM inference engine (Kwon et al., 2023), sampling 5 completions for each of 64 prompts per step over 15 epochs. We adopt verl’s default GRPO hyperparameters for each model and use the same settings across all baselines. Speculative decoding is exact, so no drafter alters the training dynamics, the sampled rollouts, or the resulting policy. The comparison therefore isolates drafting efficiency alone, and we evaluate all drafters on identical training runs.

Models: We evaluate on Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) and DeepSeek-LLM-7B (Bi et al., 2024), two popular open-weight models from different families, to demonstrate generalization.

Datasets: For our evaluation, we use GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), Spider 1.0 (Yu et al., 2018), and CodeContests (Li et al., 2022), chosen to span free-form and structured generation. GSM8K is free-form mathematical reasoning. Spider (text-to-SQL) and CodeContests (code) produce syntactically regular outputs, where cross-rollout repetition is strongest. This spread lets us characterize how acceptance scales with the regularity of the output.

Baselines: We compare against three model-free drafters under a matched draft budget of k=16k{=}16. Prompt-lookup decoding (PLD) (Saxena, 2023) drafts nn-gram continuations from the current context only. REST (He et al., 2024) retrieves continuations from a fixed datastore. SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2026) retrieves from a global suffix tree over the most recent 10k responses.

Metrics: We report tokens per decoding step (TPS): the tokens committed per target forward pass, i.e. one plus the mean accepted draft length. It is the standard lossless-speedup proxy in speculative decoding and is hardware-agnostic, so the comparison does not depend on a specific GPU or kernel. We report two aggregates: the mean over the full training run, and the mean over the final 30% of steps. We use the final 30% because training has largely saturated by this point and the cache is fully populated, which is where speculative decoding helps the most. We also plot TPS across the entire run, showing how it evolves as the policy trains.

4.1.2. Profiling Setup

Runtime measurements use a dedicated rig: Qwen3-8B (bf16, batch 64, k=16k{=}16) on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB), with a 32-core AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9970X host holding the nn-gram cache and running the lookup/scheduling chain. The throughput results (Figure 7(b)) are measured on this 8B rig. Per task, a timing pass records iteration wall-clock and hit/accept statistics, and an NVIDIA Nsight Systems (NVIDIA Corporation, 2025) pass decomposes each iteration period into device-busy time (the union of kernel, memory-copy, and CUDA-graph intervals) and exposed host time; serial host work (launch, rejection handling, cache lookup, scheduling) that are not overlapped with device execution and therefore stall the GPU.

4.1.3. Accepted-Length Comparison and Dynamics

Table 1 reports acceptance as the full-run mean and the final-30% mean. In the stable regime our cache reaches 3.6 to 7.8 tokens per step. This is a 1.21.2 to 1.99×1.99\times improvement over SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2026) and up to 7.0×7.0\times over PLD (Saxena, 2023). The overall means include our cold first epoch and still lead on every task. The advantage tracks output regularity. It is largest where completions are prompt-specific, as on Spider and DeepSeek’s GSM8K derivations. It is smallest on CodeContests, where cross-prompt boilerplate favors a global cache.

Heavy-tailed acceptance: A key benefit of our cache is that it captures long verbatim replays that other drafters miss. The mean accepted length hides a skewed distribution. Figure 5 shows the accepted length is heavy-tailed. On many steps the policy accepts most or all of the 16 draft tokens. On Spider, 12 or more are accepted on 14.1%14.1\% of steps and all 16 on up to 10.1%10.1\% (13.0%13.0\%, 6.4%6.4\%, and 3.7%3.7\% of long-accept steps on DeepSeek GSM8K, Qwen GSM8K, and CodeContests). These are verbatim replays of a prior epoch’s solution, verified in one pass. A small draft budget would forfeit them, so our large budget of k=16k{=}16 is what turns this tail into rollout speedup.

Next, we examine how acceptance evolves as training proceeds. Figure 4 shows the central dynamic on all three tasks. Acceptance is zero until prompts recur, then increases as history accumulates. On GSM8K and CodeContests acceptance strengthens throughout training. On Spider it peaks mid-run and then declines, as the policy’s SQL outputs diversify and older rollouts go stale, an effect we quantify in the window ablation below. On CodeContests the global cache leads in early training, while per-prompt history is least effective, and our cache overtakes both the baselines once that history accumulates. The redundancy is direct to measure. Consecutive-epoch rollouts of the same Spider prompt share substrings of 7 to 23 tokens, and a cache of only the earlier rollout already covers 48 to 96%96\% of the later one.

4.1.4. N-gram Cache Design Ablations

Four design choices govern the cache: two drafting hyperparameters, the maximum nn-gram order nmaxn_{\max} and the speculation length kk, and two structural choices, per-prompt keying and a bounded history window. The hyperparameters trade draft quality against cache memory, while the structural choices determine what the cache indexes and retains, and therefore where its gains come from. We ablate each in turn.

Maximum nn-gram order: As shown in Figure 6 for Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, a higher nmaxn_{\max} raises acceptance but grows the cache super-linearly, and acceptance saturates beyond order 6, so we set nmax=6n_{\max}{=}6.

Speculation length: A longer kk likewise raises acceptance until it saturates near 16, and leaves the cache unchanged, so we set k=16k{=}16. Both values sit at the knee of their speedup curves, and although Figure 6 shows one model and dataset, we find they transfer well to the others, so we use the same configuration for all experiments in the paper.

Per-prompt keying: With the drafting budget fixed, we turn to the cache’s structure. Table 2 shows the gain comes from prompt keying, not the data structure. Replacing our per-prompt keys with a single global bucket drops acceptance to 2.412.41, close to SuffixDecoding at 2.432.43, while per-prompt keying reaches 3.053.05 over the same steps. This gap is not caused by a small baseline cache. Increasing SuffixDecoding’s cache fourfold, to 40k responses, raises it only to 2.652.65. The limit is the lack of prompt-conditioned lookup, not cache size.

History window: Table 3 sweeps the per-prompt window ww, the number of recent appearances the cache retains. A window of 4 captures 79 to 91%91\% of the full acceptance at a fraction of the memory. Beyond w=16w{=}16, more history does not help and slightly lowers acceptance on GSM8K, as older rollouts go stale. This is the same drift behind Spider’s mid-run decline in Figure 4. A small window therefore saves memory and keeps the cache aligned with the current policy.

4.1.5. N-gram Prefetcher

Prefetch coverage: Figure 7(a) reports the prefetch coverage cc, the probability that the realized outcome (j∗,b∗)(j^{*},b^{*}) is among the prefetched candidates, as a function of the candidate budget NN, measured by exact replay of the saturated Qwen3-8B cache with the causal trailing-window allocator. A small budget suffices: Spider reaches c=0.95c{=}0.95 at N=8N{=}8 and saturates at 0.970.97 by N=16N{=}16, while GSM8K and CodeContests climb to 0.650.65 and 0.490.49 at N=32N{=}32 with only logarithmic gains beyond. Coverage follows the same agreement-length law as acceptance: after a full accept the bonus token is the next token of an already-cached trajectory, so high-acceptance tasks are also high-coverage tasks. The residual miss mass is entropy-limited rather than data-limited: per-step coverage plateaus within a few training steps and accumulating more rollout history does not raise it. Pushing NN past the knee therefore buys little while the prefetch-chain cost grows linearly, so we operate at N=8N{=}8–3232.

End-to-end speedup: Figure 7(b) translates coverage into wall-clock gain over the sequential synchronous baseline via Eq. (3), with TgpuT_{\text{gpu}} and TcpuT_{\text{cpu}} the CUPTI-measured device-busy and exposed-host times per decode iteration. On Spider at N=16N{=}16, Qwen3-8B achieves 1.38×1.38\times of its 1.40×1.40\times overlap ceiling (c=0.966c{=}0.966), and DeepSeek-7B, whose ceiling we measure directly at 1.21×1.21\times, achieves it outright (c=0.995c{=}0.995): near-perfect coverage makes the prefetcher equivalent to removing the host chain from the critical path, with no accepted token lost and every committed token still drawn from the target distribution. On the higher-entropy tasks the same mechanism yields 1.051.05–1.06×1.06\times against ceilings of 1.10×1.10\times (GSM8K) and 1.14×1.14\times (CodeContests); because misses fall back to the sequential lookup per request, the worst case is the baseline itself.

5. Conclusion

We presented NgramRL, a rollout-aware speculative-decoding system that exploits prompt-conditioned temporal locality in RL post-training. NgramRL builds bounded per-prompt nn-gram caches from recent policy rollouts, yielding self-updating drafts without an auxiliary model, drafter training, or GPU-resident drafter state. An adaptive fan-out prefetcher with a causal budget allocator keeps the host-resident cache off the decode critical path by preparing drafts for likely verification outcomes (j,b)(j,b), while uncovered requests fall back to sequential lookup without altering the rollout distribution. Across two model families and three workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward, up to 1.99×1.99\times more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0×7.0\times more than prompt-lookup decoding, and the prefetcher delivers up to 1.38×1.38\times measured rollout speedup over synchronous execution. These results show that recent same-prompt rollouts are an effective draft source and that outcome-aware CPU–GPU prefetching converts this temporal locality into measured acceleration while preserving exact target sampling.
